html: The two designs also behave differently under bright light. In a CCD, charge from an overfilled pixel can spill into its neighbors. This effect, called blooming, shows up as bright spots smearing across the image.[1] A CMOS sensor can handle high light levels without blooming and uses less power than an equivalent CCD. Edmund Optics' comparison also notes that CMOS has traditionally had a lower fill factor and more pixel-to-pixel variation, which lowers its signal-to-noise ratio.[1] On either sensor, blooming from over-exposure can be reduced by lowering the illumination or shortening the exposure.[1]

Every pixel captures the scene during the same time window. This makes global shutter cameras especially useful for capturing fast-moving objects, or when the camera moves rapidly during capture.[4] For example, when an eye-in-hand camera mounted on a robot wrist takes a snapshot while the arm is moving (see 2.8), a global shutter captures the moving part without spatial distortion.

However, when relative motion exists during acquisition, the time offset between rows distorts the image. Fast relative motion between the camera and object during rolling shutter acquisition causes geometric image distortion known as the rolling shutter effect.[4] For example, suppose an object moves horizontally across the field of view while rows are exposed from top to bottom. Lower rows then capture the object further along its path than upper rows. In robot guidance, this shear makes the vision system report wrong positions and orientations.

For a fixed focal length lens, three formulas tie these numbers together. With sensor width H and focal length f, the angular field of view is AFOV = 2 × arctan(H / 2f). At a working distance WD, the field of view is FOV = 2 × WD × tan(AFOV / 2). Solving for the lens gives f = H × WD / FOV.[5] These are approximations. Focal length is measured from the lens’s rear principal plane, which is rarely at its mechanical back. Treat the result as a starting point and pick the real lens from its specification table.[5] As an example, a 35 mm lens on a 2/3″ sensor (8.8 mm wide) gives an AFOV of roughly 14.5°.[5]

Ordinary lenses, called entocentric lenses, change magnification with distance. Conventional lenses have an angular field of view, which introduces parallax error: perceived magnification changes with object distance.[8] The angular field of view expands with distance. Because of this, an object closer to the lens appears larger on the sensor, while an identical object placed farther away appears smaller. For example, suppose a robotic gripper picks parts from a stack where height varies. An entocentric camera will see parts at the top of the stack as larger than parts at the bottom.

The chief rays of a telecentric lens run parallel to the optical axis. Because of this, an object's imaged dimensions stay constant even if the object moves closer to or farther from the lens within its telecentric depth of field. For example, a 20 mm shaft keeps the same image size whether it sits at the nominal working distance or shifts several millimeters along the optical axis.

Improper lighting geometry also corrupts physical measurements. Shadowing caused by improper lighting can create false edge calculations that degrade measurement accuracy.[1] For example, an overhead light source might cast an asymmetric shadow along the edge of a machined part. An edge filter can then register the shadow boundary instead of the physical edge. In pick-and-place, this false edge can shift grasping coordinates and cause gripper collisions.

Backlighting has a trade-off. While backlighting maximizes edge detection contrast, it intentionally eliminates internal surface details.[1] The front face of an opaque part receives no direct light. Features such as surface engraving, stamped serial numbers, barcode labels, and surface scratches are therefore cast into uniform shadow.

When directional or ring lights strike curved reflective surfaces, the surface acts like a curved mirror. It reflects the light source as small, saturated hot spots and leaves the rest of the part dark.

Interference filters use thin dielectric layers to pass a narrow band of wavelengths, but they have an angle-dependent artifact. Increasing the angle of incidence increases the optical path length through the dielectric layers. This shifts transmission toward shorter wavelengths in an effect known as blue shift.[6] For example, suppose an interference filter is attached to a wide-angle lens. Light at the edges of the field arrives at steep angles, which can shift the filter passband and create uneven illumination across the field.

To remove intense glare from semi-specular parts without changing lighting geometry, engineers use polarization. Cross-polarization uses a polarizer on the illumination source and an analyzer on the camera lens oriented at 90 degrees to achieve maximum rejection of unwanted glare.[6] The polarizer on the light source transmits light linearly polarized in one orientation. When this polarized light strikes a shiny surface, direct specular reflections keep their polarization orientation. They are absorbed by the analyzer filter on the lens, which is rotated 90 degrees. In contrast, light that penetrates the part surface and scatters diffusely is depolarized, allowing a portion of it to pass through the analyzer to form a clear, glare-free image.

Strobing also helps cameras with rolling shutters. As discussed in 7.1, rolling shutters expose sensor rows sequentially, creating geometric distortion when imaging moving objects. Using flash lighting is recommended on rolling shutter cameras to prevent the rolling shutter distortion effect.[8] In a darkened environment, an overdriven LED strobe can flash only during the brief window when all sensor rows expose at once. The flash then sets the exposure. The camera captures an instantaneous, undistorted snapshot of the moving object, enabling accurate robot picking and dimensional measurement.

Pick a lighting technique from this lesson for each job, and say what the camera would see. The jobs are: measuring the outer diameter of a washer; reading a label on a curved, shiny can; and finding scratches on a flat polished plate.

Choose a method from this lesson for each image, and give your reason. The cases are: dark parts on a bright, evenly lit conveyor; the same parts with a shadow across half the image; and red caps and blue caps that are equally bright.

The first conditioning stage removes points outside the robot work volume. Cameras in a cell also see fences, the floor and other equipment. The PCL PassThrough filter discards point cloud data whose coordinates along a specified axis fall outside user-defined minimum and maximum limits.[3] By setting strict bounds along the X, Y, and Z axes, the vision software trims away background structures. It isolates only the bin or conveyor zone where parts arrive.

A 3D camera can return a point for nearly every pixel, so one frame can hold hundreds of thousands of points. Every later step slows down with that many points. The PCL VoxelGrid filter downsamples point clouds by partitioning 3D space into voxel boxes and replacing all points inside each box with their centroid.[4] A voxel represents a volumetric cube in 3D space. By calculating the center of mass of all points inside each voxel cube, the filter preserves the underlying physical shape of the object while cutting the number of points.

In picking, the goal of 3D vision is a pick pose the robot can reach without collisions. Vision guidance systems use 3D point clouds for object segmentation and robot picking pose estimation via CAD model matching or geometry matching.[8] The vision software aligns a pre-loaded CAD model against an extracted cluster or analyzes local surface geometry. It then chooses a grasp point and reports the target's 6-DoF pose (X, Y, Z, Roll, Pitch, Yaw) to the robot controller.

In industrial random bin picking, robot cycles generally range from 10 to 15 seconds, allowing camera time budgets between 700 ms and 1500 ms.[8] The arm must reach into a deep bin and clear its walls. This longer cycle gives the 3D vision system up to 1.5 seconds to capture high-density scans and compute collision-free grasp trajectories.

Robotic cells frequently combine part handling with automated visual inspection. In Lesson 2.8 Vision-Guided Picking, we explored how cameras guide robot end-effectors by locating parts on tables or conveyors. Inspection builds upon those same physical setups. A camera mounted above a fixture (eye-to-hand) or on the robot wrist (eye-in-hand) captures an image of the part before or after manipulation. The robot program then checks dimensions or presence. Based on the vision verdict, the arm sorts the part into an accept bin or places it on an outbound conveyor. Alternatively, it routes the part into a quarantine station for human review.

To eliminate perspective error, precision gauging systems use telecentric lenses. Telecentric lenses eliminate parallax error in precision dimensional gauging because their non-angular field of view keeps magnification constant across changes in object distance.[5] Because of this, moving an object toward or away from the lens within its depth of field does not change its apparent size. It also leaves measured dimensions on the image sensor unchanged.

As 7.1 explained, they also help when a part drifts slightly out of focus. Because they have no angular field of view component, they blur symmetrically as focus varies, so edges keep their centroid location.[5] Sub-pixel edge detection therefore still finds the true edge.

The CC_STAT_AREA statistic output in OpenCV connected components represents the total area in pixels of the labeled component.[9] In a presence inspection application, software compares CC_STAT_AREA with upper and lower limits set during process qualification. For example, a required gasket might have an expected area of 4,500 pixels. An observed component under 3,000 pixels indicates a torn or missing gasket, which triggers an immediate robot reject routine.

For example, consider an uncompressed color camera streaming at a resolution of 1,920 columns by 1,080 rows with an encoding of “bgr8”. Each color pixel requires 3 bytes (one byte each for blue, green, and red), yielding a full row step of 1,920 × 3 = 5,760 bytes. The complete image data payload in the data byte array evaluates to 5,760 × 1,080 = 6,220,800 bytes per frame. Suppose the camera instead streams a single-channel 8-bit monochrome stream (“mono8”) at a resolution of 640 columns by 480 rows. Here each row requires exactly 640 bytes, producing a message data array of 640 × 480 = 307,200 bytes.

Understanding the distinction between width × bytes_per_pixel and the step field matters when rows are padded. In some hardware drivers and image processing pipelines, memory buffers are padded to 32-byte or 64-byte boundaries to improve memory alignment on host processors. For example, imagine a monochrome image with a width of 642 pixels. A hardware driver might pad each row to 672 bytes to satisfy memory alignment requirements. In that scenario, reading only width bytes per row would cause subsequent scanlines to drift diagonally across the raster buffer. Relying on the step field guarantees that subscriber nodes calculate row offsets accurately regardless of internal memory padding.

Intrinsic camera matrix K: The 3x3 intrinsic camera matrix K projects 3D camera frame coordinates to 2D pixel coordinates using focal lengths and principal point offsets.[3] It is stored as a 9-element row-major array [fx, 0, cx, 0, fy, cy, 0, 0, 1]. It defines horizontal and vertical focal lengths fx, fy in pixel units, along with optical principal point coordinates cx, cy.

For example, imagine a calibrated monocular camera whose intrinsic matrix K has focal lengths fx = 800.0, fy = 800.0 pixels and principal point offsets cx = 320.0, cy = 240.0 pixels. Suppose a workpiece corner is located at physical 3D camera coordinates [X, Y, Z] = [0.10 m, 0.05 m, 1.00 m]. Under ideal pinhole projection, the normalized coordinates evaluate to x' = X / Z = 0.10 and y' = Y / Z = 0.05. Multiplying by the focal lengths and adding the principal point offsets gives the pixel coordinates. The horizontal pixel coordinate is u = 800.0 × 0.10 + 320.0 = 400.0 pixels. The vertical pixel coordinate is v = 800.0 × 0.05 + 240.0 = 280.0 pixels. When lens distortion is present, downstream rectification nodes use the coefficients in D alongside matrix K. They remap raw distorted pixels into ideal rectilinear coordinates described by matrix P.

A single 1080p uncompressed color stream at 30 frames per second generates over 180 megabytes per second of raw data. Multiple perception nodes might subscribe to an uncompressed camera topic across an industrial Ethernet switch or wireless network. In that case, the physical bus can become saturated, resulting in dropped packets and processing jitter.

The cv_bridge package converts in both directions, handling memory buffers, channel order, and color conversion. In cv_bridge, imgmsg_to_cv2 converts a ROS Image message into an OpenCV NumPy image with an optional desired_encoding format.[6] You can specify the desired_encoding parameter (such as "bgr8" or "mono8"). The camera hardware might transmit data in RGB, BGR, or Bayer formats. Regardless of the input format, this ensures the output NumPy array is converted into the exact memory layout expected by your OpenCV algorithms.

An OpenCV pipeline analyzes or annotates an image matrix. The resulting NumPy array often needs to be re-published onto the ROS 2 network for visualization in RViz2 or logging with ros2 bag. In cv_bridge, cv2_to_imgmsg converts an OpenCV image array into a ROS Image message with a specified pixel encoding string.[6] This function formats the NumPy array into a compliant sensor_msgs/msg/Image message. It includes calculated row step bytes and matching encoding metadata, ready for immediate publication.

In this hands-on lab exercise, you will implement an end-to-end Python ROS 2 node. It subscribes to an incoming camera stream and converts image messages with cv_bridge. It then applies OpenCV color conversion, binary thresholding, and Canny edge detection, and publishes the processed results.

Once an image is converted to single-channel intensity, binarization isolates candidate foreground workpieces from the background fixture or conveyor. Simple binary thresholding with cv.threshold assigns pixels above a threshold value to maxval and all other pixels to zero.[8] For example, consider setting a threshold parameter of 128 with a maximum value of 255. All bright workpiece pixels exceeding 128 are assigned to 255 (pure white), while darker background pixels are assigned to 0 (pure black).

Put the script in an ament_python package the same way as in 4.6. Add rclpy, sensor_msgs and cv_bridge as dependencies in package.xml. Next, register the script as an entry point, then build with colcon and source the workspace. If cv_bridge is missing, install ros-lyrical-cv-bridge.

Check that the distortion model specifies plumb_bob, and that the distortion parameters array d contains the five coefficients [k1, k2, t1, t2, k3]. Also check that intrinsic matrix k and projection matrix p contain non-zero focal lengths and principal point values.

In industrial automation, discrete input and output signals operate primarily on direct current. Sinking and sourcing terminology applies only to DC input and output circuits.[1] Alternating current (AC) circuits reverse polarity continuously, so sinking and sourcing concepts do not apply to them. Direct current circuits maintain fixed positive and negative polarities. Sinking or sourcing input and output points can conduct current in one direction only.[1] Wiring devices to a PLC or robot controller therefore means knowing which way current enters and leaves each terminal. Current flows in one direction only through solid-state switches and optical isolators.

In contrast, other types of operational information are exchanged only occasionally. Acyclic communication transmits diagnostic data on an as-needed basis rather than adhering to a fixed cyclic update schedule.[4] For example, an operator might upload an error log from a motor drive, modify a controller parameter, or read temperature trends. These actions happen only when an operator requests them or a fault event triggers them. These requests are answered when they arrive instead of on a fixed schedule.

Data production in a CIP network is managed to make efficient use of network bandwidth. Digital input modules on CIP networks produce data either upon a change of state or at a requested packet interval.[2] Change-of-state (COS) transmission lets a sensor module transmit as soon as an input turns from off to on, without waiting for a polling cycle. The requested packet interval (RPI) defines the cyclic rate at which data is regularly produced regardless of state changes.

PROFINET (Process Field Network) is an industrial Ethernet technology from PROFIBUS & PROFINET International (PI). This organization is a global network of vendors, developers, system integrators and users that promotes and advances the technology.[3]

In Lesson 8.3 Lab: Connecting a Robot to a PLC, you will put these principles into practice. You will write and read holding registers from a Python client, using a stand-in for a robot's Modbus TCP server.

Match each description to a protocol from this lesson. First: a single frame passes through every device, which reads and inserts data on the fly. Second: implicit I/O data travels over UDP and explicit requests over TCP. Third: big-endian registers on TCP port 502.

As 8.2 covered, Modbus TCP messages carry a 7-byte MBAP header over TCP port 502.[3] Its data model has four tables (discrete inputs, coils, input registers and holding registers), with values sent big-endian.[4] The function codes below work on the two 16-bit register tables: input registers are read-only, while holding registers can be read and written.

In pymodbus, a client object is created with ModbusTcpClient and connects to the target device using the connect method.[7] By default, the pymodbus ModbusTcpClient connects using socket framing on default port 502.[7] When created, the client accepts the target host IP address and network port, then opens a TCP socket to the server.

The client wrote value 1 to register 128 with function code 0x06. It then wrote values 250 and 7 to registers 129 and 130 with function code 0x10. Finally, it verified the writes by reading all three registers back with function code 0x03.

This lesson covers four technologies that sit at different levels. IO-Link works at the sensor level. OPC UA and MQTT deliver machine data to IT systems. Finally, ROS 2 serves as a robot software framework that connects to all of them.

Nodes represent objects, variables, and executable methods. References connect nodes into an address space graph. For example, a robot controller's OPC UA server could model an arm as a parent Object node named RobotArm. It contains child Object nodes for each axis (Joint1 through Joint6). Each joint provides Variable nodes for position and velocity with engineering units, alongside Method nodes to trigger calibration routines.

For example, consider a vision-guided sorting cell. A ROS 2 computer can plan the arm's motions through ros2_control. Meanwhile, a separate node on the same computer reads part pick counts and publishes those metrics to factory dashboards over MQTT or OPC UA.

Secure DMZ communication models require control zones to push data to the DMZ and enterprise users to pull data from DMZ application servers.[2] For example, the cell sends its production records to a server in the DMZ. An office application then reads them from that server, so nothing in the office ever connects to the robot.

A virtual LAN divides physical networks into smaller logical broadcast domains that isolate traffic from other VLANs.[2] For example, you can assign robot motion traffic to VLAN 20 and human-machine interface (HMI) traffic to VLAN 30. This keeps high-volume display graphics from interfering with motion control packets on the same physical switch hardware.

Modbus TCP messages include a 7-byte MBAP header and transmit over TCP on registered port 502.[9] The MBAP header contains four fields. These are the Transaction Identifier (2 bytes), the Protocol Identifier (2 bytes, set to 0 for Modbus), the Length field (2 bytes indicating remaining bytes), and the Unit Identifier (1 byte). Because the test server runs on port 5020 rather than the registered port 502, you will configure Wireshark to decode that port.

Manufacturers generate maintenance records documenting equipment faults, failures, root causes, and repairs to speed up troubleshooting and improve failure prediction.[2] Technicians should keep a maintenance log for each robot, recording what was seen, what was done, and the root cause. This lets the next technician check whether the same symptom has happened before.

Universal Robots recommends a service check at one of its regional service centers “at least bi-annually”.[3] The page does not say whether that means twice a year or every two years, so ask your distributor.

Freedrive (pulling the arm into position by hand, see 2.1): set the correct TCP, payload and center of gravity. Next, move the arm to a stretched-out horizontal position and check that it holds its position.

Label each case reactive, preventive or predictive. Case one: a gripper is replaced after it fails in the middle of a shift. Case two: grease is changed every 12 months whatever the condition. Case three: a joint is serviced because its motor current has been rising for a month.

This system includes the manipulator, controller, end effector, part fixtures, and supervisory programmable logic controllers (PLCs).

The main tool is a digital multimeter (DMM). Technicians should ohm out multimeter test leads before testing to verify the resistance measurement is close to zero.[1] To do this, set the meter to resistance and touch the probe tips together.

Fuses will not save a sensor from a wiring mistake. Fast-acting fuses and electronic current-limiting circuits operate too slowly to protect solid-state sensors from short circuits or reverse polarity wiring.[4]

A robot only knows where its joints are if its position sensors and stored calibration data agree with the real arm. (1.6 Robot Anatomy and Coordinate Frames covers the joints.) After some repairs that agreement is lost and has to be restored. This lesson uses ABB's and Universal Robots' procedures as examples; always follow the manual for your own robot.

Choosing mock hardware or Gazebo. Start with mock hardware: it is the lightest option and enough to test planning and the MTC stage chain. Know its limits. UR's simulation page lists several mock hardware limits: there is no TCP pose broadcaster, and the passthrough trajectory controller and force mode do not work. In addition, the GPIO (general-purpose input/output) controller reports a failure when you try to set I/O.[4] So if you planned to open and close a gripper through UR digital outputs, you cannot check that in mock mode.[4] Gazebo adds a physics simulation and comes with its own MoveIt launch (milestone 4).[5]

How MTC thinks. MTC splits a task into stages of three kinds.[1] Generators create states on their own (the current state, candidate grasp poses). Propagators take a neighbour's state and push it forward or backward ("move 10 cm up"). Connectors plan a free motion between two states that already exist. Stages can be grouped in containers: wrappers, serial containers and parallel containers.[1] MTC also has three planners (solvers) a stage can use. These are a Cartesian planner for straight-line moves, joint interpolation for simple moves, and the full planning pipeline using OMPL (the Open Motion Planning Library, which provides sampling-based path planning algorithms). The tutorial uses joint interpolation for the simple hand move.[1]

In this capstone you build a small machine that holds a wheel at a speed you choose, in revolutions per minute (RPM), and keeps it there when the load changes. An Arduino reads a quadrature encoder on a DC gearmotor, works out the wheel speed, and runs a PID loop that sets the PWM duty cycle sent to an H-bridge driver. A state machine wraps the loop. The wheel ramps up gently, runs under PID control, and ramps back down. It drops into a FAULT state if something goes wrong, such as a stalled shaft or a lost encoder signal.

Every closed-loop axis has the same parts, from a hobby robot's drive wheel to a joint inside an industrial arm (see the nested servo loops in 6.4). It needs a sensor that measures motion and a controller that compares it with a target. It also needs a power stage to drive the motor, and supervisory logic that decides when the loop may run at all. Lessons in Chapter 6 taught these parts one at a time. Here you join them, measure how well the result works, and write up what you learned.

If you write your own interrupt service routine (ISR) instead, follow the Arduino rules. Attach it with attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(pin), ISR, mode), where mode is LOW, CHANGE, RISING or FALLING. Keep it short, and declare any variable shared with loop() as volatile. Inside an ISR, delay() does not work and millis() does not advance.[4] A multi-byte count can change halfway through being copied, so copy it between noInterrupts() and interrupts(). The library handles this for you.

Worked example: at the 30:1 motor's no-load speed of about 330 RPM,[5] the output turns 5.5 times per second. The encoder therefore produces about 5.5 × 1920 = 10 560 counts per second, or about 1056 counts in a 100 ms sample. One count in a 100 ms window is worth 60 000 / (1920 × 100) = 0.3125 RPM, which is the resolution of your speed reading. With a 10 ms window, one count would be worth 3.125 RPM, so short windows give coarse, jumpy speed readings.

Open loop first. Before adding feedback, drive the motor with fixed duty cycles and record the speed. analogWrite() takes values from 0 to 255. An industrial arm is bolted down, so every position can be measured from its base (1.6). A mobile robot has to work out where it is before it can plan a route. This chapter uses Nav2, the ROS 2 navigation project introduced in 3.5 Case Study: Contributing to Nav2, as its worked example. It also builds on the wheel odometry in 6.6 Odometry.

Planners and controllers are at the heart of a navigation task.[1] Nav2 runs them inside action servers. Five of its action servers are the planner, behavior, smoother, route and controller servers, which host the algorithm plugins that do the work.[1]

The nav2_waypoint_follower sends the robot to several destinations and has a plugin interface for a task at each one, such as taking a picture, picking up a box or waiting for user input.[1] Nav2 describes two schools of thought for fleets: a dumb robot with a smart centralized dispatcher, or a smart robot with a dumb one.[1] In the first approach, a request to the waypoint follower is one unit of work, such as one pick in a warehouse. The robot then returns to the dispatcher for its next task.[1]

For each job, name the Nav2 server that does it. First: finding a way across the building. Second: steering around a cart that has just been left in the aisle. Third: freeing the robot after its costmap fills with obstacles that are not there.

Driving across a building takes time, so Nav2 is built on ROS 2 actions. Action servers are a common way to control long-running tasks: a client requests a task, the server provides feedback while it runs, and a result comes back at the end.[1] For navigation, the request may be a position. The feedback may be the time spent navigating and the distance to the goal, and the result is a boolean for success.[1]
